title.value: Pressure Build Up and Drawdown Behavior in Undersaturated Reservoirs of Discontinuous Permeability

name.value: Stanford University, Department of Petroleum Engineering

note.value: Transient pressure testing is used extensively as a means of determining formation flow capacity and extent of well damage around producing wells., Analytical expressions developed for evaluating the results of pressure testing are based generally upon the assumption of homogeneous rock properties, even though reservoir inhomogeneities such as faulting, lensing, stratification, fracturing, and anisotropy introduce anomalies in the pressure test data and may affect the accuracy of calculations. This thesis presents the results of an investigation of skin effect evaluation in reservoirs having horizontal and vertical permeability variations.A numerical technique was developed to simulate a single well in an infinite horizontal reservoir, For radial symmetry, the problems were solved with a two-dimensional mathematical model in r-z geometry. The Alternating Direction Implicit Procedure provided the basis of the numerical solution of finite difference equations <> The simulation model was verified by comparing the results with analytical solutions of simple reservoir systems where possible, and then was used to evaluate more complex systems having vertical and horizontal permeability discontinuities These systems included: fractured reservoirs, stratified reservoirs, composite reservoirs, and lenticular reservoirs. In addition, the model was used to simulate partial penetration and selective completion in reservoir systems of variable vertical and horizontal permeability. The primary goal of this study was to determine if the usual methods of evaluating skin effect and formation flow capacity were applicable to certain heterogeneous reservoir systems.Analysis of results from the mathematical models indicate that when vertical permeability variation (stratification) exists, the determination of skin effect and flow capacity may be performed in the usual manner. On the other hand, whenever radial discontinuities exist, as in composite systems, it was found that considerable differences in computed values and actual values of skin effect result. These differences were construed to be another form of skin effect attributed to the radial changes in permeability. A method was developed for determining true skin effect in the presence of radial discontinuities. It gives reliable results in composite and lenticular reservoir systems. Skin effect evaluations in partially-penetrated reservoirs may be made by applying the Brons and Marting pseudo-skin effect correction factorsÑ It was found, however, that it was necessary to multiply this resulting skin effect by the fractional penetration to give the true skin effect upon which remedial programs should be based. This correction results from the fact that flow rates through the damaged region increased proportionally to the reciprocal of the fractional penetration.With respect to partially penetrated wells, it was found that horizontal fractures and shale barriers influence pressure performance in a manner that can be treated as a skin effect. The total skin effect of the system is the sum of the individual skin effects attributed to well damage, partial penetration, and fracture or shale barrier, as the case may be. Here again the true skin effect to be used in designing remedial programs is obtained after correcting for the increased flowrate through the damaged region as described above.

Rowland, David Andrew. (1969). Pressure Build Up and Drawdown Behavior in Undersaturated Reservoirs of Discontinuous Permeability. Stanford Digital Repository. Available at: https://purl.stanford.edu/qj205fc7922
